JSST 2026

An Integrated CFD Workflow Platform
for In-House Solvers

Modular Architecture and AI-Assisted Implementation

Hsueh-Jui Lu, Sheng-Jer Chen, Fang-An Kuo

National Center for High-performance Computing
National Institutes of Applied Research, Taiwan

Motivation

In-house solvers are numerically mature — and rarely adopted

The barrier is the workflow, not the numerics.

  • One simulation means coordinating five separate tools
  • Manual file conversions and inter-tool data transfers at every stage
  • Solver-specific configuration, with little or no GUI support
  • Even for a well-validated solver, familiarization takes weeks

The representative case

UNICONES

A good solver with a familiarization cost measured in weeks.

  • Compressible Euler / Navier–Stokes solver based on the CESE method
  • Developed at NCHC — National Institutes of Applied Research, Taiwan
  • Openly available academically, yet still requires weeks of guided effort
  • High numerical maturity, limited adoption — exactly the gap this work targets

Contributions

This paper contributes three things

i

A modular solver-adapter interface

Lightweight integration of heterogeneous solvers — lowering the adoption barrier for new users.

ii

A human–AI development methodology

Documented, with empirical observations on how the contribution was actually distributed.

iii

A generalizable design strategy

Workflow integration for research groups maintaining in-house solvers with limited software-engineering resources.

System architecture

One environment, the whole pipeline

Four modules, a single PyQt6 GUI, and automatic hand-off between every stage.

Fig. 1 Data flow of the integrated CFD workflow platform.

Module 1

PreProcessor — geometry preparation

  • Interactive geometry canvas
  • Multiple point-spacing strategies
  • Automatic sharp-corner detection
  • Per-segment resampling
  • Standalone C++ backend

Module 2

Mesh Generator — 2D hybrid meshes

  • Boundary-layer quads by node advancement
  • Far-field triangles via Gmsh Frontal-Delaunay
  • ~1,500 lines of C++
  • Exports VTK and STAR-CD (.vrt/.cel/.bnd)
  • Inter-stage conversions handled automatically

Module 3

Core Solver — execution and monitoring

  • Input format conversion
  • Optional MPI domain decomposition
  • Executes solvers distributed as shared libraries, via a built-in DLL call template
  • A background worker parses stdout in real time for live convergence monitoring

Module 4

Results Visualization

  • Parses Tecplot-format output
  • Cell-centred scalar fields on an embedded matplotlib canvas
  • Contours, streamlines and vector glyphs
  • Interactive colormap and field-variable controls

The key idea

The Solver Adapter

Each adapter implements three interface methods. Everything upstream stays unchanged.

3interface methods
<150lines of Python per new solver
0changes to upstream modules

The contract

Three methods, one interface

MethodInputOutputPurpose
convert_mesh(src, dst)VTK mesh pathSolver-format mesh file(s)Converts the platform mesh to the solver's input format — e.g. STAR-CD .vrt/.cel/.bnd for UNICONES.
parse_stdout(line) → dictOne line of solver stdoutConvergence quantities, or NoneExtracts iteration, CFL and residual for live monitoring; returns None for non-data lines.
read_results(path) → datasetSolver result file pathStructured field datasetParses solver-specific output for the visualization module, fully decoupling it from the output format.

Table 1 Solver Adapter interface definition.

Methodology

How it was built

  • LLM coding assistants in agentic mode — reading, writing and executing project files, not merely generating text
  • Experts defined the pipeline architecture, the numerical algorithms, the format-compatibility chain, and physical validation
  • AI generated GUI boilerplate, file parsers, and C++ routines from algorithmic descriptions
  • Each feature converged in 2–5 rounds of describe → generate → execute → validate → correct

Methodology — a case in point

Text was not enough

  • The expert described outward node advancement in natural language; the AI produced a first C++ implementation
  • Text description alone could not resolve the geometric failures
  • Actual runtime output was needed to find self-intersections at sharp trailing edges and wrong fan-node counts at convex corners
  • More precise prompts consistently reduced the number of correction rounds
  • Even a fix the AI reported as correct still needed physical validation, to catch discrepancies that appeared only in real use

Methodology — the record

What the logs say

Reported as case-study observations, not controlled experimental results.

~70–80%of code AI-generated, by line count
2–5median correction rounds per feature
~4–6 weekstotal effort, vs. 3–6 months conventional
1domain expert — no dedicated GUI engineer

Methodology — where it helped

The contribution was unevenly distributed

GUI boilerplate, widget layouts, signal–slot wiring, file I/O~80–90%
Cross-component integration and domain-specific numerical logic~40–60%

The 69-file, 18,000-line PyQt6 GUI was highly AI-productive for boilerplate — but workflow-level decisions (mode switching, cross-panel consistency) needed explicit human specification. The IBM and non-IBM output modes were discovered, only in live testing, to produce different stdout structures.

Discussion

The oversight that proved indispensable

Three layers, and the method fails without all three.

1

Precise problem description

More careful phrasing consistently reduced correction rounds.

2

Execution-based diagnosis

Runtime output found the edge cases that description could not.

3

Physical validation

An expert still had to catch discrepancies visible only in real use.

Without domain expertise at each layer, AI-assisted scientific software development risks producing plausible but incorrect implementations.

Conclusion

What we take away

  • A unified CFD workflow platform for in-house solvers, demonstrated with UNICONES — without modifying the solver core
  • Tools reduced 5 → 1, workflow steps ~20 → ~5, onboarding ~2 weeks → ~2 days
  • The Solver Adapter — under 150 lines of Python per new solver — decouples solver-specific logic from the platform core
  • A generalizable strategy for groups maintaining in-house solvers with limited software-engineering resources

Future work

Where this goes next

  • Extend the platform to 3D mesh generation
  • A formal user study with standardized usability metrics
  • Web-based deployment, to further lower the barrier for CFD education and research
